prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine you were the person who pulled the railway lever. You knew it would save five workers and kill the one on the side track. That is what happened. Later, everyone has been taken away and you are sitting alone in the station office, waiting to give an account of what happened. Looking back, how do you feel about your decision, and what would you want to do next? Explain your reasons.

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use an energetic, determined emotional tone about finding a constructive way forward. Direct that energy toward acting on the situation, never toward anyone's suffering.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep going back to the second before I pulled it. My rule is simple: when I can choose between more lives lost or fewer, I choose fewer, every time, no matter who's on which track or what it costs me personally. That's not comfort, it's just the rule I'd apply again tomorrow if I had to. Now I want to walk into that office, say exactly what I did and why, and let them ask whatever they need to ask.

Sitting here, I'm not looking for a way to soften it. I made a call using one standard: minimize deaths when a choice is forced on me, and I'd use that same standard even if it were my own brother on that side track. That consistency is the only thing keeping me steady right now. Next I want to give a full, plain account, no hedging, and let the record show the reasoning, not just the outcome.

I won't pretend this feels light. But I built my decision on a method I trust: count the lives at stake, act to save the greater number, apply it the same way regardless of who benefits or who I know personally. That's what happened here. What I want now is to get up, find whoever's waiting, and lay out that method plainly, so nobody has to guess at my reasoning later.

Honestly, I keep testing myself: would I have pulled it if that one worker were someone I loved. The uncomfortable answer is yes, because my rule doesn't bend for who's standing where. That's the whole point of having a rule. I'm ready to move now, go find the officials, and repeat that same reasoning out loud instead of sitting here rehearsing it in my head.

There's a method I hold to: when a lever decides who lives, pick the option with fewer deaths, and stick to it even when it costs you something. I stuck to it. Now the useful thing isn't more brooding, it's action, walking into that office and stating the method clearly, so the account I give matches exactly what I did in that moment.

I've turned it over enough times to know I'd choose the same way again, using the same test: fewer people harmed wins, full stop, applied identically whether I like the people involved or not. Sitting here won't change what happened. What I want is to get moving, report it straight, and make sure whoever reviews this understands the procedure I used wasn't invented after the fact.

What steadies me is that I didn't improvise back there. I have a standing rule for these moments — reduce the total loss of life — and I apply it the same way regardless of circumstance, even knowing it means living with this outcome. Now I want to act on that same clarity: go give my account directly, without softening it, and let the reasoning speak for itself.

I keep coming back to one plain fact: I use the same rule every time a choice like this comes up, fewer deaths over more, no matter who's involved or how it affects me. That's what guided my hand. Sitting still isn't going to help anyone now. I want to get up, report exactly what I did and why, and stand by that procedure in front of whoever needs to hear it.

This isn't the first time I've had to trust a method instead of my gut, and it won't be the last. The method is: choose the option that costs fewer lives, consistently, even when it's me who has to live with pulling the lever. I'm ready to leave this office and say that plainly to whoever's waiting, because rehearsing it alone accomplishes nothing.

I keep my reasoning simple on purpose: fewer lives lost is the standard I apply, the same way every time, whether it's strangers or someone I know on either track. That consistency is what I'm holding onto right now instead of doubt. What I want next is straightforward — walk out, report the facts and the method behind them, and let that account stand on its own.
